name: Roam Research
tagline: Outliner for networked thought: daily notes, bidirectional links, and block references.
description: Roam Research is an outliner for networked thought: daily notes, bidirectional links, and block references that any page can quote.
pros: Daily notes make capture the default action, so a thought can be written before deciding where it belongs
Block references let one passage be quoted from another page while staying attached to its origin
Bidirectional links mean a page is found from every page that mentions it, without filing anything twice
The outline model keeps a research draft and its supporting fragments in one continuous, indentable structure
Rated 4.3 out of 5 from 2,200 reviews in this repository's recorded data
cons: The habit is the cost: links and daily capture only pay off with discipline, and an unlinked graph becomes a second pile of unread pages
Structured layouts, databases, and task boards sit outside the outline model, so formatted output is produced somewhere else
The corpus lives in a hosted service with a limited free plan recorded, and this repository stores no compliance certifications for Roam Research

content.title: Daily notes as the entry point
content.body: Roam starts each day on a dated page. The note-taking comparison in this repository records daily notes as the default entry point, with pages created as needed as writing continues, which inverts the usual habit of deciding where a note belongs before writing it. Capture happens first and structure emerges afterward: a thought lands under today, gets indented, and later acquires links to pages elsewhere. For research work that arrives in fragments, readings, interviews, half-formed arguments, that is a lower-friction starting point than choosing a notebook.

content.title: Blocks, links, and how a page is built
content.body: The unit below the page is the block. This repository records Roam Research as pioneering the outliner approach with bidirectional linking and block-level referencing, and describes block referencing as allowing any block of text to be referenced from any other note. The consequence is that a passage can be quoted somewhere else while staying attached to its origin, so an argument assembled from scattered sources keeps its provenance. The recorded mechanics of a page are listed below.

content.title: An outline, not a document
content.body: Because everything is an outline, structure comes from indentation and links alone; formatted layouts and structured databases are not part of the model. That is workable for prose still being figured out and awkward for material that wants columns, properties, or a fixed template. The same repository entry that credits Roam with pioneering block-level referencing is describing a tool optimized for thinking in progress rather than for producing finished, formatted artifacts. Buyers should read that as a commitment: if the output has to look like something, this is the drafting layer, not the publishing one.

content.title: What networked thought asks of you
content.body: The features are cheap to start and expensive to sustain. Daily capture only pays off if links are made consistently, and a graph built without discipline becomes a second pile of unread pages, because the tool records connections but does not tidy them. Block references also make pages demanding to maintain: a note that quotes six other places needs attention when those places change. This repository positions Roam for knowledge workers who benefit from bidirectional linking and daily notes, which describes the reader it wants as accurately as it describes the habit it demands.

content.title: What the subscription record shows
content.body: This page records Roam Research as paid with a band of $15-50/mo, and that is the one figure the record quotes for this product. The note-taking comparison in this repository adds the model behind it: a subscription, with a free plan of limited functionality and paid plans that include unlimited blocks, file uploads, and collaboration features. Because blocks are the unit of work, the free ceiling is felt quickly by anyone writing daily. Confirm current list pricing with the vendor before committing a research budget to it.

content.title: Hosted notes, and what is not on file
content.body: Roam is delivered as a hosted service: the graph lives on the vendor's infrastructure and is reached through a browser rather than as a folder on your machine. The dataset returns no compliance certification when searched for Roam Research and no such entry is written here; readers refer to the documentation the vendor currently publishes. For a user whose entire research corpus sits in one hosted graph, the questions worth pressing are about how complete an export is, what happens to linked references if the subscription lapses, and where the data resides.

content.title: Evernote, Obsidian, Notion, and the stray pairings
content.body: Nine pages of comparisons in this repository feature Roam Research. Four are the real argument, Evernote, Obsidian, Notion, and Todoist, where the choice is between a capture store, a local vault, a workspace database, and a task list. The remaining pages pair Roam with Acuity Scheduling, Cal.com, Calendly, JotForm, and Typeform, which sell scheduling and forms, so they read as directory breadth rather than rivalry. The Roam Research alternatives file lists Todoist, Evernote, and Obsidian as the closest substitutes on record.

content.title: Who should write in Roam
content.body: Roam suits researchers, PhD writers, and analysts whose material arrives as fragments and who will keep linking it, which is the audience this repository's note-taking guidance names directly. It suits individuals who want capture and connection in the same surface and do not need a formatted deliverable out of the other end. It does not suit teams that need shared documents with permissions, or buyers who want their notes as local files. This reading is based on this repository's stored records and Roam's published product material; nobody here has written inside Roam. Those records show 4.3 out of 5 from 2,200 reviews.

faqs.question: What is a block reference in Roam?
faqs.answer: Any block of text can be referenced from any other note, per this repository's note-taking comparison, so a passage can be quoted elsewhere while staying tied to its origin.

faqs.question: Where does a Roam session start?
faqs.answer: The daily notes page. This repository records daily notes as Roam's default entry point, with pages created as needed as the writing continues.

faqs.question: Is there a free version of Roam Research?
faqs.answer: A limited one. This page records Roam as paid with a band of $15-50/mo, and the comparison records a free plan of limited functionality alongside paid unlimited blocks and uploads.

faqs.question: How is Roam different from Obsidian?
faqs.answer: Both link notes bidirectionally. Roam is an outliner of hosted pages built on daily notes and block references, while Obsidian edits a folder of Markdown files stored on your own device.

faqs.question: What is Roam actually for?
faqs.answer: This repository's note-taking guidance positions it for knowledge workers who benefit from bidirectional linking and daily notes: research, synthesis, and long-form argument built from fragments.

author: Sarah Chen
learningCurve: High relative to a notebook, because the daily-notes and block-linking habit has to be learned before the graph is worth anything
whoShouldUse: Researchers, writers, and analysts who work in fragments and will keep linking them: people who want capture and connection on the same surface and do not need a formatted deliverable at the end.
whoShouldNotUse: Teams that need shared documents with permissions, buyers who want notes as local files, and individuals who will not maintain the daily-linking habit the model rewards.
